---
title: Evaluating predictions in R
author: Diplodocus Contributors
---

Tiny Stats compares predictions with observed values. This walkthrough computes
error scores and plots residuals so you can see which observations account for
the error.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tinystats)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

## Start with predictions

Suppose a model predicts four responses. The first three predictions match their
observations, but the last prediction is too high.

```{r predictions}
observed <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
predicted <- c(1, 2, 3, 6)
errors <- residuals(observed, predicted)
errors
```

[`residuals`] subtracts each prediction from its observation. A negative residual
means the model predicted too high. Here, the last residual is `r tail(errors, 1)`.

## Compare error scores

[`mean_squared_error`] averages the squared residuals,
$\mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$.
[`mean_absolute_error`] averages their absolute values. Squaring gives larger
errors more weight, while absolute error stays in the response's units.

```{r scores, results='asis'}
scores <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Mean squared error", "Mean absolute error",
             "Root mean squared error", "Mean error", "R squared"),
  Value = c(mean_squared_error(observed, predicted),
            mean_absolute_error(observed, predicted),
            root_mean_squared_error(observed, predicted),
            mean_error(observed, predicted),
            r_squared(observed, predicted))
)
knitr::kable(scores, digits = 2)
```

The mean squared error is `r mean_squared_error(observed, predicted)`, and the
mean absolute error is `r mean_absolute_error(observed, predicted)`. The mean
error of `r mean_error(observed, predicted)` indicates that predictions are too
high on average. R squared compares the squared error with the variation in the
observations; it requires observations that are not constant.

## Inspect residuals

A single score can hide where a model fails. Plot the residuals against the
observations and use the zero line to identify exact predictions.

```{r residual-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap='The last prediction accounts for all of the error.', fig.alt='Three residuals are zero; the residual for observed value four is minus two.'}
plot(observed, errors, pch = 19, col = "#2563eb",
     xlab = "Observed value", ylab = "Residual", ylim = c(-2.5, 0.5))
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
```

All of the error comes from the last observation. Check this case before using
the average scores to judge the model. For larger datasets, look for trends,
changing spread, or groups of unusual residuals.

Read [Choosing a metric](../../docs/guides/choosing-a-metric.md) for the tradeoffs
between scores, or use [`root_mean_squared_error`] to report a score in the
response's units.
